items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "spontaneous change"?
options: A change that, once started, takes place without a continuous supply of energy from outside the system.
The entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero is zero, so all substances have positive standard entropies at 298 K.
S: a measure of the dispersal of energy and of the number of possible arrangements of particles and their energy (disorder) in a system.
S°: the entropy of 1 mole of a substance in its standard state at 298 K and 1 bar, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
items.answer: A change that, once started, takes place without a continuous supply of energy from outside the system.
items.markingKey: Spontaneous change: a change that, once started, takes place without a continuous supply of energy from outside the system.

items.stem: For which reaction is ΔS most positive?
items.answer: NH₄Cl(s) → NH₃(g) + HCl(g)
items.markingKey: Two moles of gas from a solid.

items.stem: For H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g), why is ΔS small?
options: The number of moles of gas does not change
items.answer: The number of moles of gas does not change
items.markingKey: 2 mol gas → 2 mol gas.

items.stem: What is the sign of the entropy change, ΔS, for heating 1 mol of copper from 300 K to 500 K?
options: Positive, because particles vibrate more; more ways to distribute energy
Negative, because particles vibrate more; more ways to distribute energy
Positive, because the reaction is exothermic
items.answer: Positive, because particles vibrate more; more ways to distribute energy
items.markingKey: ΔS is positive: particles vibrate more; more ways to distribute energy.

items.stem: Predict the sign of ΔS for each change and explain your predictions: (i) NH₄NO₃(s) + aq → NH₄⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq); (ii) heating 1 mol of copper from 300 K to 500 K.
items.answer: (i) positive: solid lattice breaks into dispersed ions; (ii) positive: particles vibrate more; more ways to distribute energy.
items.markingKey: each sign [1]; each reason referring to states / moles of gas / disorder [1] [4]

items.stem: Lina is studying the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) (ΔH° = −92 kJ mol⁻¹). Standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): N₂(g) 191.6, H₂(g) 130.6, NH₃(g) 192.3. (a) Calculate ΔS° for the reaction. (b) Explain why the standard entropy of a gas is much larger than that of a solid.
items.answer: (a) −198.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (b) Gas particles move randomly and are widely spaced, with many more possible arrangements of particles and energy.
items.markingKey: (a) ΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants) = (2 × 192.3) − (191.6 + 3 × 130.6) [1]; −198.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) Gas particles move randomly and are widely spaced [1]; with many more possible arrangements of particles and energy [1] [2]

items.stem: Which substance has the highest standard molar entropy at 298 K?
items.answer: CO₂(g)
items.markingKey: Gases have much higher entropy than liquids or solids.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "third law of thermodynamics"?
options: S°: the entropy of 1 mole of a substance in its standard state at 298 K and 1 bar, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
The entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero is zero, so all substances have positive standard entropies at 298 K.
ΔS: the difference between the total entropy of the products and of the reactants, ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants).
S: a measure of the dispersal of energy and of the number of possible arrangements of particles and their energy (disorder) in a system.
items.answer: The entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero is zero, so all substances have positive standard entropies at 298 K.
items.markingKey: Third law of thermodynamics: the entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero is zero, so all substances have positive standard entropies at 298 K.

items.stem: Explain why the entropy of a substance increases sharply at its boiling point.
items.answer: At the boiling point the liquid becomes a gas; the particles become much more spread out with many more possible arrangements and energy distributions, so entropy jumps.
items.markingKey: change of state to gas [1]; many more arrangements [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why dissolving an ionic solid in water usually has a positive entropy change.
items.answer: The ordered lattice breaks up and the ions disperse throughout the solution, increasing the number of possible arrangements (though water molecules become ordered around ions).
items.markingKey: The ordered lattice breaks up and the ions disperse throughout the solution [1]; increasing the number of possible arrangements (though water molecules become ordered around ions) [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the standard entropy of diamond is lower than that of graphite.
items.answer: Diamond is a rigid three-dimensional lattice with strong bonds in all directions, so its atoms have fewer ways of vibrating/arranging energy than graphite, whose layers can slide and vibrate more freely.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Diamond is a rigid three-dimensional lattice with strong bonds in all directions; so its atoms have fewer ways of vibrating/arranging energy than graphite; whose layers can slide and vibrate more freely (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): N₂(g) 191.6, H₂(g) 130.6, NH₃(g) 192.3. What is ΔS° for the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)?
items.answer: −198.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

items.stem: What is the sign of the entropy change, ΔS, for C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g)?
options: Negative, because the reaction is exothermic
Positive, because two moles of gas become one
Negative, because two moles of gas become one
items.answer: Negative, because two moles of gas become one
items.markingKey: ΔS is negative: two moles of gas become one.

items.stem: Standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): H₂(g) 130.6, O₂(g) 205.0, H₂O(l) 69.9. What is ΔS° for the reaction 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)?
items.answer: −326.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Predict the sign of ΔS for each change and explain your predictions: (i) NH₄NO₃(s) + aq → NH₄⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq); (ii) 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).
items.answer: (i) positive: solid lattice breaks into dispersed ions; (ii) negative: a gas is used up, forming a solid.
items.markingKey: each sign [1]; each reason referring to states / moles of gas / disorder [1] [4]

items.stem: Sipho is studying the reaction 2NO₂(g) → N₂O₄(g) (ΔH° = −57 kJ mol⁻¹). Standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): NO₂(g) 240.0, N₂O₄(g) 304.2. (a) Calculate ΔS° for the reaction. (b) Explain why all the standard entropy values are positive.
items.answer: (a) −175.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (b) All substances above 0 K have some disorder (particles vibrate / have energy to distribute); only a perfect crystal at 0 K has S = 0.
items.markingKey: (a) ΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants) = (304.2) − (2 × 240.0) [1]; −175.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) All substances above 0 K have some disorder (particles vibrate / have energy to distribute); only a perfect crystal at 0 K has S = 0 [1]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by entropy and describe how the entropy of a system changes with temperature, change of state and changes in the number of moles of gas. Include how ΔS is calculated from standard entropies.
items.answer: Entropy = dispersal of energy / number of arrangements; increases with temperature (more energy states); large jumps at melting and especially boiling; gases ≫ liquids > solids; reactions producing more moles of gas have positive ΔS; dissolving usually positive; ΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants) with units J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; worked example.
items.markingKey: definition [1]; temperature [1]; changes of state [2]; moles of gas [1]; calculation with units [2] [7]

items.stem: Isla is studying the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g) (ΔH° = −196 kJ mol⁻¹). Standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): SO₂(g) 248.1, O₂(g) 205.0, SO₃(g) 256.7. (a) Explain why the standard entropy of a gas is much larger than that of a solid. (b) Calculate ΔG° at 298 K and state whether the reaction is feasible at this temperature.
items.answer: (a) Gas particles move randomly and are widely spaced, with many more possible arrangements of particles and energy. (b) ΔG° = −196 − 298 × (−0.1878) = −140.0 kJ mol⁻¹; feasible
items.markingKey: (a) Gas particles move randomly and are widely spaced [1]; with many more possible arrangements of particles and energy [1] [2] (b) ΔS in kJ [1]; ΔG value [1]; conclusion [1] [3]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "feasible reaction"?
options: ΔG°: the Gibbs free energy change for a reaction under standard conditions.
Temperature measured in kelvin, used for T in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
A reaction for which ΔG is negative (or zero), so it can take place without continuous input of energy.
The situation in which a reaction is feasible (ΔG negative) but does not occur at a measurable rate because the activation energy is high.
items.answer: A reaction for which ΔG is negative (or zero), so it can take place without continuous input of energy.
items.markingKey: Feasible reaction: a reaction for which ΔG is negative (or zero), so it can take place without continuous input of energy.

items.stem: ΔG for the combustion of methane is very negative, but methane does not burn at room temperature without a spark. Why?
options: ΔG is positive at room temperature
The activation energy is high, so the rate is negligible
items.answer: The activation energy is high, so the rate is negligible
items.markingKey: ΔG says nothing about rate.

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH = +50 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Which is correct?
options: It is feasible at all temperatures
It is not feasible at any temperature
items.answer: It is not feasible at any temperature
items.markingKey: Both terms make ΔG positive.

items.stem: For the reaction Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g), ΔH° = −25 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = +15.2 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG at 700 K?
items.answer: −35.6 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: For the reaction ZnO(s) + C(s) → Zn(s) + CO(g), ΔH° = +238 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = +189.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔG at 1000 K and state whether the reaction is feasible at this temperature.
items.answer: +48.1 kJ mol⁻¹; not feasible

items.stem: Use the standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): Fe₂O₃(s) 87.4, CO(g) 197.6, Fe(s) 27.3, CO₂(g) 213.6, and ΔH° = −25 kJ mol⁻¹, to calculate ΔG for Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g) at 298 K. State whether the reaction is feasible at this temperature.
items.answer: −29.5 kJ mol⁻¹; feasible

items.stem: Elena is evaluating making water gas from coke: C(s) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + H₂(g), ΔH° = +131 kJ mol⁻¹. Standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): C(s) 5.7, H₂O(g) 188.7, CO(g) 197.6, H₂(g) 130.6. (a) Calculate ΔS° for the reaction. (b) Suggest two reasons why the actual temperature used may differ from your calculated value.
items.answer: (a) +133.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (b) ΔH and ΔS vary with temperature (values are for 298 K); a higher temperature is needed for a reasonable rate; conditions are not standard (e.g. product gases removed).
items.markingKey: (a) ΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants) = (197.6 + 130.6) − (5.7 + 188.7) [1]; +133.8 [1] [2] (b) any 2 from: ΔH and ΔS vary with temperature (values are for 298 K); a higher temperature is needed for a reasonable rate; conditions are not standard (e.g. product gases removed) (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Kenji is evaluating producing magnesium oxide for refractory bricks: MgCO₃(s) → MgO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH° = +117 kJ mol⁻¹. Standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): MgCO₃(s) 65.7, MgO(s) 26.9, CO₂(g) 213.6. (a) Calculate ΔS° for the reaction. (b) Calculate ΔG° at 298 K and comment on the feasibility of the reaction at room temperature.
items.answer: (a) +174.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (b) +64.9 kJ mol⁻¹; not feasible at 298 K

items.stem: A reaction is feasible when
items.answer: ΔG is negative
items.markingKey: ΔG ≤ 0 for a feasible change.

items.stem: In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, what units must ΔS have if ΔH is in kJ mol⁻¹?
items.answer: kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: Divide J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ by 1000.

items.stem: State the equation linking ΔG, ΔH, T and ΔS.
items.answer: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
items.markingKey: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS [1]

items.stem: Explain why a reaction with a negative ΔG may not take place at room temperature.
items.answer: ΔG shows only that the reaction is thermodynamically feasible; if the activation energy is high the rate is extremely slow (kinetically stable).
items.markingKey: ΔG relates to feasibility only [1]; high Ea / slow rate [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why ΔS must be divided by 1000 when calculating ΔG.
items.answer: Standard entropies are given in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ but ΔH is in kJ mol⁻¹; units must be consistent.
items.markingKey: Standard entropies are given in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ but ΔH is in kJ mol⁻¹; units must be consistent [1]

items.stem: Explain how an endothermic reaction can be feasible.
items.answer: If ΔS is positive and large enough, at a high enough temperature TΔS exceeds ΔH, so ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative.
items.markingKey: positive ΔS [1]; TΔS > ΔH at high T [1] [2]

items.stem: Ethan says: "All exothermic reactions are feasible." Explain whether Ethan is correct.
items.answer: An exothermic reaction with a negative ΔS becomes non-feasible at high temperature when TΔS outweighs ΔH.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: An exothermic reaction with a negative ΔS becomes non-feasible at high temperature when TΔS outweighs ΔH. [2]

items.answer: +171.1 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH negative and ΔS negative. Under what conditions is it feasible?

Feasible only at low temperatures (below T = ΔH/ΔS)
items.answer: Feasible only at low temperatures (below T = ΔH/ΔS)

items.answer: +64.9 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH positive and ΔS positive. Use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS to explain how the feasibility of the reaction depends on temperature. An example is 2Fe₂O₃(s) + 3C(s) → 4Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g).
items.answer: Feasible only at high temperatures (above T = ΔH/ΔS): ΔH is positive but −TΔS is negative and grows with T; at high T it outweighs ΔH.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "Faraday constant"?
options: F: the charge on 1 mole of electrons, 96 500 C mol⁻¹.
E°cell: the e.m.f. of a cell under standard conditions, E°(reduction electrode) − E°(oxidation electrode).
The temperature at which ΔG = 0, given by T = ΔH ÷ ΔS, above or below which a reaction becomes feasible.
Whether a reaction can occur in terms of energy, shown by ΔG ≤ 0 or E°cell > 0.
items.answer: F: the charge on 1 mole of electrons, 96 500 C mol⁻¹.

items.stem: Why does the feasibility of an exothermic reaction with negative ΔS decrease as temperature increases?
items.answer: The −TΔS term becomes more positive
items.markingKey: It eventually outweighs ΔH.

items.stem: The unit of ΔG° from ΔG° = −nFE°cell, with F in C mol⁻¹ and E in V, is

items.answer: −474.8 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: For the cell reaction Mg(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Zn(s), E°cell = +1.61 V. Calculate ΔG° for the reaction in kJ mol⁻¹. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹)
items.answer: −310.7 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Lucas in Colombo builds an electrochemical cell based on the reaction Zn(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s), which has E°cell = +1.56 V. (a) Explain what the signs of E°cell and ΔG° show about the reaction. (b) Suggest why the reaction might not be observed when the reagents are mixed, even though ΔG° is negative. (c) State the relationship between ΔG and the cell e.m.f. under non-standard conditions.
items.answer: (a) E°cell positive and ΔG° negative: the reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions. (b) The activation energy may be high so the rate is very slow; or concentrations are not standard. (c) ΔG = −nFE, using the measured cell e.m.f. E.
items.markingKey: (a) E°cell positive and ΔG° negative: the reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions [2] [2] (b) The activation energy may be high so the rate is very slow; or concentrations are not standard [1] (c) ΔG = −nFE, using the measured cell e.m.f; E [1]

items.answer: Negative

items.stem: Explain why a reaction with positive E°cell might still not be observed.
items.answer: Positive E°cell (negative ΔG) shows thermodynamic feasibility, but the activation energy may be high so the rate is negligible; non-standard concentrations may also change E.

items.stem: Explain why the decomposition of calcium carbonate is feasible only at high temperatures.
items.answer: ΔH is positive and ΔS is positive; ΔG becomes negative only when TΔS exceeds ΔH, i.e. above T = ΔH/ΔS (about 1100 K).
items.markingKey: ΔH is positive and ΔS is positive [1]; ΔG becomes negative only when TΔS exceeds ΔH, i.e. above T = ΔH/ΔS (about 1100 K) [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why ΔH and ΔS are assumed constant when the threshold temperature is calculated.
items.answer: Standard values are measured at 298 K; they change a little with temperature, so the calculated T = ΔH/ΔS is an approximation.
items.markingKey: Standard values are measured at 298 K [1]; they change a little with temperature, so the calculated T = ΔH/ΔS is an approximation [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the sign of the entropy change, ΔS, for NH₄NO₃(s) + aq → NH₄⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq)?
options: Negative, because solid lattice breaks into dispersed ions
Positive, because solid lattice breaks into dispersed ions
Positive, because the reaction is exothermic
items.answer: Positive, because solid lattice breaks into dispersed ions
items.markingKey: ΔS is positive: solid lattice breaks into dispersed ions.

items.stem: Use the standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): C(s) 5.7, H₂O(g) 188.7, CO(g) 197.6, H₂(g) 130.6 to calculate ΔS° for the reaction C(s) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + H₂(g).
items.answer: +133.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Omar is studying the reaction CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) (ΔH° = +178 kJ mol⁻¹). Standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): CaCO₃(s) 92.9, CaO(s) 39.7, CO₂(g) 213.6. (a) Predict, without calculation, the sign of ΔS° for this reaction. Explain your prediction. (b) Explain why the standard entropy of a gas is much larger than that of a solid.
items.answer: (a) Positive: more moles of gas / more disordered products. (b) Gas particles move randomly and are widely spaced, with many more possible arrangements of particles and energy.
items.markingKey: (a) sign [1]; reason [1] [2] (b) Gas particles move randomly and are widely spaced [1]; with many more possible arrangements of particles and energy [1] [2]

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH negative and ΔS positive. When is it feasible?
items.answer: At all temperatures

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH negative and ΔS positive. Under what conditions is it feasible?
options: Feasible only at high temperatures (above T = ΔH/ΔS)
Feasible only at low temperatures (below T = ΔH/ΔS)
items.answer: Feasible at all temperatures
items.markingKey: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS: feasible at all temperatures.

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH positive and ΔS negative. Under what conditions is it feasible?

items.answer: Never feasible

items.stem: Leila is evaluating formation of nitrogen monoxide in a car engine: N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g), ΔH° = +181 kJ mol⁻¹. Standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): N₂(g) 191.6, O₂(g) 205.0, NO(g) 210.7. (a) Calculate the minimum temperature at which the reaction becomes feasible. (b) Suggest two reasons why the actual temperature used may differ from your calculated value.
items.answer: (a) 7300 K (b) ΔH and ΔS vary with temperature (values are for 298 K); a higher temperature is needed for a reasonable rate; conditions are not standard (e.g. product gases removed).
items.markingKey: (a) ΔG = 0 so T = ΔH ÷ ΔS [1]; = +181 ÷ (+0.0248) = 7300 K [1] [2] (b) any 2 from: ΔH and ΔS vary with temperature (values are for 298 K); a higher temperature is needed for a reasonable rate; conditions are not standard (e.g. product gases removed) (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: For the reaction Br₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Br⁻(aq) + I₂(aq), ΔG° = −106 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate E°cell. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹)

Lina in Kathmandu builds an electrochemical cell based on the reaction Mg(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Zn(s), which has E°cell = +1.61 V. (a) Explain what the signs of E°cell and ΔG° show about the reaction. (b) Suggest why the reaction might not be observed when the reagents are mixed, even though ΔG° is negative. (c) Describe and explain how E for the cell would change if the concentration of a reactant ion were increased. (d) State the relationship between ΔG and the cell e.m.f. under non-standard conditions.
items.answer: (a) E°cell positive and ΔG° negative: the reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions. (b) The activation energy may be high so the rate is very slow; or concentrations are not standard. (c) E becomes more positive: the equilibrium at that electrode shifts to the right (Le Chatelier / Nernst), so the reaction becomes more feasible and ΔG more negative. (d) ΔG = −nFE, using the measured cell e.m.f. E.
items.markingKey: (a) E°cell positive and ΔG° negative: the reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions [2] [2] (b) The activation energy may be high so the rate is very slow; or concentrations are not standard [1] (c) E more positive [1]; reason [1] [2] (d) ΔG = −nFE, using the measured cell e.m.f; E [1]
